analysis.one_liner: Requires agencies to analyze rules' costs to small businesses and makes finished rules easier to challenge in court.
analysis.headline: Introduced on the first day of the 115th Congress and referred to two House committees, the bill never received a vote in either chamber and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Regulatory Flexibility Act, the 1980 law that requires federal agencies to study how their rules affect small businesses. It would widen the definition of 'rule' to cover more agency actions, require more detailed impact studies that count indirect effects, strip agencies' authority to skip those studies, let small-business groups get earlier access to drafts, and allow lawsuits over the analyses as soon as a rule is published. It would also require agencies to periodically review existing rules and consider amending or rescinding them. The practical effect would be slower rulemaking and more legal openings to challenge federal rules on everything from workplace safety to environmental protection.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses gain a bigger role in rulemaking, review panels before rules are proposed, and new grounds to sue agencies in court. Larger regulated companies also gain, because the bill's expanded definition of 'economic impact' counts indirect effects on small entities even when a rule does not directly regulate them, giving big firms a procedural handle to contest rules through small-business claims.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every agency to prepare detailed regulatory flexibility analyses covering direct and reasonably foreseeable indirect economic effects on small entities, including effects on compliance costs, revenue, credit access, and energy costs.

Eliminates agencies' existing authority to waive or delay the initial flexibility analysis, and lets the SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy convene review panels and intervene in agency proceedings before rules are finalized.

Moves the deadline to sue an agency over the quality of its small-business analysis to the moment a rule is published, rather than after the rulemaking process ends, and lets affected small entities obtain the review-panel report and supporting materials within 10 business days of asking.
Requires each agency to publish a plan to review all rules with significant effects on small entities within 10 years and to consider amending or rescinding them.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules — workers, consumers, patients, and communities protected by workplace, environmental, financial, and product-safety regulations — would bear the cost as slower, more litigation-exposed rulemaking delays or weakens those protections. Federal agencies would also bear heavy new analysis, reporting, and litigation-defense duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal regulations

drawbacks.text: Expanding analyses to indirect effects and removing waiver authority would add time and paperwork to rulemaking across agencies, delaying rules that protect workers, consumers, and the environment.

Allowing judicial review as soon as a rule is published creates an early window to sue over the adequacy of an agency's small-business analysis, a vulnerability that applies regardless of the size of the businesses actually affected, since the bill requires counting indirect effects on small entities even when the rule does not directly regulate them.

The bill's stated rationale is helping small businesses, but nothing in the analysis requirements limits their use to genuinely small firms; a large company can invoke small-entity impacts in its supply chain to slow a rule that applies to it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Genuine small-business participation in rulemaking has real value, and some of the bill — plain-language summaries, soliciting input from affected firms, outreach to women-, veteran-, and minority-owned businesses — is uncontroversial. But the bill's central changes, mandatory indirect-effect analyses, no waivers, and immediate judicial review, are procedural tripwires that mainly make rules easier to delay or strike down, and the burden falls on the public's regulatory protections rather than on any regulated party.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Small Business committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a Judiciary subcommittee nine days later, and was never reported out, marked up, or voted on by either chamber before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Chabot and 13 original cosponsors introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the opening day of the 115th Congress.
The Speaker referred it to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Small Business Committee the same day, and to a Judiciary subcommittee on January 12, 2017.
Sixteen members cosponsored the bill, 15 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

The Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship held a hearing on the subject in March 2017, printing S.Hrg. 115-21, but no Senate bill action followed and the House never voted on H.R. 33.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies kept their existing rulemaking procedures, and the regulatory protections that the bill would have made slower and easier to challenge remained in force. Regulated businesses did not get the expanded litigation tools.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors but one were Republicans, and the bill's core aim — more analysis requirements and easier legal challenges to agency rules — matched the Republican conference's regulatory agenda; no Democratic support beyond Rep. Henry Cuellar appeared on the record.

industries.industry: Large regulated industries (energy, finance, manufacturing, chemical and other companies subject to federal rules)
industries.note: The bill requires agencies to count indirect effects on small entities even when a rule does not directly regulate those entities, and allows lawsuits as soon as a rule is published. That gives large companies a procedural route to slow or contest rules through small-entity impact claims, at the cost of delayed protections for the public.

Small firms would get earlier access to draft rules, review panels, mandatory consideration of their costs including credit and energy costs, and periodic agency review of existing rules. The benefit is real but comes bundled with a litigation framework whose largest users would be big companies.

Agencies would lose waiver authority, gain mandatory indirect-impact and quantification analyses, face earlier judicial review, and must report annually on rule reviews to Congress and the SBA. Their institutional interest in carrying out the statutes Congress assigned them runs alongside the public's interest in timely rules.
